classification.difficultyReason: Heights must be found from a circle of radius 6, giving surds (3√3), then the trapezoidal rule in exact form, then π is extracted. Part b adds a concavity explanation. It is a linked multi-step task, but a cleaner one than the calculus-based p29-q12, whose values are decimals.

content.prompt: The diagram shows the semicircular entrance of a tunnel, divided into four strips of equal width.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use the trapezoidal rule to estimate the area of the entrance. Give your answer in exact form.

answer.worked:
The semicircle has centre $O$ and radius $6\text{ m}$, so $y=\sqrt{36-x^2}$ and $h=3$. At $x=-6,-3,0,3,6$ the heights are $0,3\sqrt3,6,3\sqrt3,0$.
$$\begin{align*}A&\approx\frac{3}{2}\bigl[0+0+2(3\sqrt3+6+3\sqrt3)\bigr]\\&=3(6\sqrt3+6)\\&=(18+18\sqrt3)\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Use part a to approximate $\pi$. Give your answer correct to one decimal place, and explain why your approximation is less than $\pi$.

answer.short: $\pi\approx1+\sqrt3\approx2.7$ (1 d.p.). The curve is concave down, so the chords lie below it and the trapezoidal rule underestimates the area.
answer.worked:
The area of the semicircle is $\dfrac12\pi(6)^2=18\pi$.
$$\begin{align*}18\pi&\approx18+18\sqrt3\\\pi&\approx1+\sqrt3\\&\approx2.7\quad\text{(1 d.p.)}\end{align*}$$
The curve is concave down, so each trapezium lies below the curve. The area estimate is too small, so the approximation of $\pi$ is less than $\pi$.
